description: A crooked, many-stemmed shrub with smooth, polished red-brown bark and stiff, round, pale gray-green (almost white) leaves held edge-on to the sun; 1.5-3.5 m tall here. It grows in chaparral and in openings of the woodland and pine forest on dry, rocky ridges, and its late-winter flowers are among the first nectar of the year for hummingbirds and native bees, while its berries feed birds, foxes, coyotes and bears.

season_notes.winter: Flowering in late winter (February-March): small white-to-pink urn-shaped flowers, early nectar for hummingbirds and native bees.
season_notes.spring: Flowers give way to sticky green berries.
season_notes.summer: The berries ('little apples', which is what manzanita means) ripen red-brown, and the red bark peels in thin curls.
season_notes.fall: Evergreen and dormant through the dry season; next winter's flower buds are already set at the branch tips.

notes: Common manzanita of foothill chaparral and the understory of open oak and pine woodland, 1-4 m. An obligate seeder (no burl): a short base divides at once into several crooked, stiff, upswept stems (stems 3-5 spreading 35 degrees, high curve variance, upward tropism). Bark smooth, polished red-brown to mahogany, peeling in thin curls: the most recognisable thing about it, so the bark colour is saturated and the bark pattern smooth. Branching is sympodial with terminal inflorescences (Leeuwenberg's model): each shoot ends in a flower cluster and growth continues from lateral buds below it, which gives the forked, zigzag look. Leaves 2-5 cm, oval to round, thick, glaucous whitish grey-green, and held vertically (edge-on to the midday sun): orientation 'vertical'. Flowers white to pink, January-April, which lightens the spring colour. Evergreen.
